name: James River
subtitle: From the bay to the Fall Line
intro: Captain your little survey boat inland on the James. Find safe channels, deliver supplies, and discover why rivers shaped Virginia. At Richmond, the river will ask you to find a new way forward.
historicalContext: This is an imagined learning expedition, not a reenactment. Indigenous peoples lived along and traveled these waterways long before English colonists founded Jamestown in 1607. Their communities continue today.

legs.name: The wide tidal James
legs.objective: Follow the deep blue channel. Steer around driftwood and pale shallows.
legs.arrival: Cross the gold landing line anywhere in the channel. Your boat docks automatically.
legs.journal: Jamestown was founded by English colonists in 1607 on the James River, upstream from its Chesapeake Bay connection. The river offered deep-water access for ships. This was already Indigenous homeland.
legs.observation: Broad tidal water connects the James to the Chesapeake Bay. Tides can change local currents.
legs.landingIntro: You have reached Jamestown on the James River. Your boat is safely moored. Complete the docking log, read a field note, then prepare camp with five more questions.

fieldNote.title: A foothold on the James
fieldNote.text: English settlers established Jamestown in 1607 in the Coastal Plain. The Virginia Company hoped to earn money. Deep water let ships approach, but unhealthy drinking water and food shortages threatened survival. Trade with Powhatan communities helped provide food. Tobacco later became a valuable crop for sale.

legs.name: The river is a road
legs.objective: Carry your supplies inland. Read the bends and line up with the open water.
legs.arrival: Cross the gold landing line anywhere in the channel. Your boat docks automatically.
legs.journal: You brought cargo straight to a river landing. Navigable rivers connected settlements to supplies and trade. The supply landing in our game is fictional; its connection to the water demonstrates a real geographic advantage.
legs.observation: A landing connects boats to people on shore. Rivers moved both people and goods.
legs.landingIntro: Your boat has reached our expedition supply landing. This stop is fictional, but using a river to move goods is part of Virginia’s real history.

fieldNote.title: A river full of trade
fieldNote.text: Colonial farms sent tobacco to river wharves for shipment to England. A crop grown for sale is a cash crop. Ships brought tools and other supplies back. Farmers depended on buyers, and a failed harvest could reduce their income. Enslaved people and indentured servants performed much of the difficult labor behind this trade.

legs.name: The river changes
legs.objective: Rockier water ahead. Slow down to find gaps; the current pushes against you.
legs.arrival: Cross the gold landing line anywhere in the channel. Your boat docks automatically.
legs.journal: Richmond sits at the Fall Line between the Coastal Plain and Piedmont. Rapids interrupt river navigation. Transferring goods between water and land helped trading centers grow.
legs.observation: More exposed rock and stronger current: you are approaching Richmond's Fall Line.
legs.landingIntro: You have reached Richmond at the Fall Line. The rocks and rapids you approached explain why cargo may need a different route.

fieldNote.title: Where the landscape changes
fieldNote.text: At Richmond, the James crosses the Fall Line. This boundary separates the rolling Piedmont to the west from the lower Coastal Plain to the east. Falls and rapids interrupted navigation by large ships. Moving goods onward could require unloading and a different route.

legs.journal: You changed from boat travel to carrying cargo on land. A portage is a way to move a boat or its cargo around an obstacle. Our short shore trail represents that idea; it is not a real marked route through Richmond.
legs.observation: The water is still moving, but your cargo follows a land route around the obstacle.
legs.landingIntro: You carried the cargo around the rapids and reached base camp. This is an imagined camp, not a marked real-world portage route.
